summary:
Syria's Penal Code criminalises the conduct a trans visitor may be read as engaging in. Article 520 of the 1949 code prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" and carries up to three years' imprisonment; Article 517 covers public indecency. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that both provisions reach men and women alike, so a trans visitor is reachable under the same articles irrespective of legal sex marker or presentation.

Legal gender recognition is not available in Syria, LGBTI organisations cannot register, and no anti-discrimination protection exists in any field. The state's response to same-sex conduct is criminalisation, which removes the complaint route a visitor would otherwise have after an assault, a refusal of service or a document dispute.

Enforcement has fallen on private gatherings. In June 2010 Syrian authorities raided several private parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men, most charged with "homosexual acts" and others with drug offences; the same crackdown included charges of encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Syria Direct reported on 11 October 2020 that homosexuality and public-decency offences remain illegal in Damascus, where a resident described meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes "only in whispers."

Violence against LGBT Syrians has also come from non-state armed actors. A Human Rights Watch report of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021) tallied at least 16 killings claimed by ISIS in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016, and reported that the Islamic State said it executed at least 30 people for "sodomy" in areas under its control, an issue raised at the UN Security Council in August 2015 in the Council's first-ever discussion of LGBTQ concerns. Beatings and torture of LGBTQ people by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State are documented in the same record.

Political actors have endorsed harsher treatment: Free Syrian Army member Nasradeen Ahme stated he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, while secular leader Miral Bioredda said Syrian society would say "no way" to gays claiming rights.

Public cultural expression has been squeezed since the civil war. The region's only gay tour, covering Damascus and Aleppo, stopped operating; the underground LGBTQ hubs of Damascus have been eradicated; and the hammams of Aleppo and Damascus that served as the tour's main venues no longer function in that role. Digital expression persists anonymously: the "One of you" movement began on Facebook in March 2020 and moved to Twitter, with participants using fake accounts for fear of identification, and it faded amid COVID-19.

Health care access is shaped by official stigma. In 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly called HIV/AIDS "divine punishment" for fornication and homosexuality, while the Health Ministry claimed only 369 people were infected, a figure NGOs estimated at least five times too low, and the UN chastised the government for ineffective prevention. The state runs voluntary HIV testing clinics and offers a limited HIV/AIDS educational program in secondary schooling, but comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist. Prevalence was under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1% among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 reported cases through Q3 2019 since the first reported infections in 1987.

A GEM (Guardians of the Gem) report of April 2025, working through an on-the-ground reporter network, investigated and found inaccurate a report claiming LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs, debunking it to avoid stirring incitement against the community. The most recent enforcement incident in this record remains the 2010 party raids; no later state raid is documented here.
tangentialFactors:
Two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the UN Security Council, a closed session co-sponsored by the United States and Chile reported by Newsweek in 2015, describing constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.

In the diaspora, Syrian LGBTQ+ refugees face discrimination and exclusion in host countries based on race, language, skin colour and religious background. Abdulrahman Akkad, a Syrian young man in Germany, came out publicly on Facebook in July 2017 while under family pressure to marry against his will, and his case was raised in the German Parliament's 2020 human rights session. The 2017 film Mr. Gay Syria follows two gay Syrian refugees rebuilding their lives.

Earlier literary expression includes Nizar Qabbani's 1971 poem "The Evil Poem," describing a relationship between two women.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, no ability to register an LGBTI organisation, and no anti-discrimination protection in any field. LGBT Syrians describe life at home as constrained to whispers: a 36-year-old, Amira al-Tabbaa, told Syria Direct on 11 October 2020 that she meets friends in gay-friendly cafes "only in whispers."

The state runs voluntary HIV testing clinics, distributes pamphlets, tolerates the work of some NGOs, and offers a limited HIV/AIDS educational program for youth in secondary schooling; comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist. Physical safety is also a care barrier, with beatings and torture of LGBTQ people documented, including attacks by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State.

Youth are both a target and an organising force. University students in the "One of you" movement painted LGBTQ flag colours on their fingers and photographed themselves by a faculty building under #oneofyou, most using fake accounts for fear of being identified; reactions ranged from defence to threats of blood before it faded amid COVID-19.
outOfScopeNotes:
The EUAA Syria country-focus page on treatment by state, non-state and societal actors yielded no usable finding recorded for Syria in this inventory; its content is unresolved here.

The most recent state enforcement incident documented in this record is the June 2010 party raids; no later raid by state authorities is sourced, and the April 2025 GEM report addresses a specific debunked claim about Homs rather than documenting current state practice. An undocumented present is not a safe present.

ISIS and Islamic State execution figures (at least 16 killings claimed as of June 2016; at least 30 executions reported) are raw counts without denominators and without a per-capita comparison to Syria's general homicide rate during the same period, so their magnitude relative to background violence is unresolved.

HIV prevalence figures (under 2 per 100,000 general population, under 1% most-at-risk, 1,013 cases through Q3 2019) are national health statistics whose relationship to trans-specific care access is not sourced here.
